The manipulation of time in the story is masterfully balanced and serves the emotional core of the narrative. The author uses **stretching of time** during the shooting in the synagogue—an event that likely lasted only seconds in story time is drawn out over several paragraphs to capture Barbara's shock, sensory details, and internal thoughts (such as remembering the dead bird on the steps or noticing the youth of the shooter's face). This effectively mimics how trauma slows down perception.

Conversely, the author uses **compression of time** in the second half of the story to show how the aftermath of the trauma lingers and gradually fades into the background of everyday life. Weeks are condensed into short sentences ("The snow softened and refroze. Her husband had the car serviced."), and later, years and decades are compressed into a few brief paragraphs covering the birth and growing up of her daughter. This contrast between the stretched moment of crisis and the compressed years of recovery creates a poignant, realistic rhythm that highlights how a single brief moment can echo across an entire lifetime.
